systemic: Affecting or involving the body as a whole rather than one isolated organ or area.
SLE is systemic because it can affect the skin, joints, kidneys, blood, lungs, heart, and nervous system.
systemic lupus erythematosus: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system makes antibodies that cause inflammation and may damage multiple organs, especially the skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, heart, lungs, and nervous system.

Look for fatigue, joint pain, photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, low blood counts, and kidney involvement. ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are more specific. Monitor urine and renal function, reinforce sun protection and medication adherence, and teach infection precautions when immunosuppressed.
SLE: The standard abbreviation for systemic lupus erythematosus, a chronic autoimmune disease that can affect multiple organs.

Assess for skin and joint symptoms, fatigue, cytopenias, and kidney involvement. ANA is sensitive but not diagnostic alone; anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, complement levels, urinalysis, and renal function help evaluate disease activity.
lupus: An autoimmune disease that causes inflammation; systemic lupus erythematosus is the best-known systemic form and can affect multiple organs.
Important nursing concerns include photosensitivity, joint pain, fatigue, rash, low blood counts, and lupus nephritis. Reinforce sun protection and monitoring for organ involvement.
erythematosus: A medical adjective associated with erythema (redness); it is part of the name systemic lupus erythematosus.
In SLE, the term appears in the disease name and is associated with inflammatory skin findings such as a malar rash.
lupus nephritis: Inflammation of the kidneys caused by systemic lupus erythematosus.
Foamy urine, proteinuria, blood in the urine, edema, hypertension, or rising creatinine may signal kidney involvement. Monitor urinalysis and renal function.
photosensitivity: An abnormal skin reaction to sunlight or ultraviolet light.
Sun exposure can trigger or worsen lupus skin symptoms. Teach protective clothing, sunscreen, and avoiding intense UV exposure.
malar rash: A red rash across the cheeks and bridge of the nose, sometimes called a butterfly rash.
It is a possible finding in SLE but is not present in every client and is not diagnostic by itself.
ANA: A blood test that detects antibodies reacting with structures in the cell nucleus.
ANA is sensitive for SLE but not specific; a positive result can occur in other conditions and some healthy people. Interpret with clinical findings.
anti-dsDNA: An autoantibody directed against double-stranded DNA that is relatively specific for SLE.
It can support an SLE diagnosis and may rise with disease activity, particularly kidney involvement.
anti-Smith: An autoantibody highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, although not present in every client.
A positive result supports SLE; it is not a reliable measure of disease activity by itself.
cytopenia: A lower-than-normal number of one or more types of blood cells.
SLE can cause anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia. Monitor CBC and assess for fatigue, infection, bruising, or bleeding.
proteinuria: An abnormal amount of protein in the urine.
It can indicate kidney damage, including lupus nephritis. Monitor urine protein and renal function.
Addison disease: A disorder in which the adrenal cortex cannot produce enough cortisol and often not enough aldosterone.
Common findings include fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and sometimes hypoglycemia. Clients need hormone replacement and stress-dose teaching.
primary adrenal insufficiency: Failure of the adrenal cortex to produce adequate cortisol and often aldosterone; Addison disease is the usual chronic form.
Low cortisol with high ACTH is typical. Low aldosterone can cause sodium loss, potassium retention, dehydration, and hypotension.
Addisonian crisis: A life-threatening acute lack of adrenal hormones, often triggered by infection, surgery, trauma, vomiting, or missed steroid replacement.
Suspect severe hypotension, weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or hypoglycemia. Emergency treatment includes IV hydrocortisone and isotonic fluids.
adrenal crisis: A life-threatening state caused by inadequate cortisol during physiologic stress or acute adrenal failure.
Recognize shock, severe weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, altered mental status, and electrolyte/glucose abnormalities. Do not delay emergency glucocorticoids and IV fluids.
ACTH stimulation test: A test that measures how the adrenal glands respond to synthetic adrenocorticotropic hormone.
Cortisol is measured before and after ACTH. An inadequate cortisol rise supports adrenal insufficiency.
ACTH: A pituitary hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol.
ACTH is usually elevated in primary adrenal insufficiency and low or inappropriately normal in secondary adrenal insufficiency.
adrenalectomy: Surgical removal of one or both adrenal glands.
After surgery, monitor blood pressure, fluid/electrolyte balance, glucose, and signs of adrenal insufficiency. Bilateral removal requires lifelong hormone replacement.
cortisol: A glucocorticoid hormone made by the adrenal cortex that supports the stress response, blood glucose, blood pressure, and regulation of inflammation.
Too little cortisol can cause adrenal insufficiency; too much can cause Cushing syndrome. Long-term steroid therapy can suppress natural cortisol production.
aldosterone: A mineralocorticoid hormone that helps the kidneys retain sodium and water and excrete potassium.
Low aldosterone can cause hypotension, dehydration, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia.
Cushing syndrome: A condition caused by prolonged exposure to excessive cortisol, from the body's production or from glucocorticoid medication.
Findings may include central weight gain, rounded face, thin skin, easy bruising, muscle weakness, hypertension, hyperglycemia, and increased infection risk.
acromegaly: A disorder caused by excess growth hormone after the growth plates have closed, usually from a pituitary tumor.
It causes gradual enlargement of hands, feet, jaw, and facial features and can contribute to diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea, and cardiac disease.
gigantism: Excess growth hormone before the growth plates close, causing unusually rapid linear growth and very tall stature.
Unlike acromegaly, gigantism occurs during childhood/adolescence while bones can still lengthen.
Graves disease: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid gland, causing hyperthyroidism.
Possible findings include weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, goiter, and sometimes exophthalmos.
thyroid storm: A life-threatening, extreme worsening of thyrotoxicosis with severe hypermetabolism.
Suspect high fever, marked tachycardia, agitation or delirium, vomiting/diarrhea, and possible heart failure. It is an emergency.
myxedema coma: A life-threatening decompensation of severe hypothyroidism, often triggered by infection, cold exposure, or sedatives.
Findings include hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, and decreased level of consciousness.
methimazole: An antithyroid thionamide medication that reduces thyroid hormone synthesis.
Teach the client to report fever or sore throat immediately because agranulocytosis is a rare but serious risk.
propylthiouracil: An antithyroid medication that reduces thyroid hormone synthesis and decreases conversion of T4 to active T3.
A serious risk is liver injury; report jaundice, dark urine, right-upper-quadrant pain, or severe fatigue. Fever or sore throat may signal agranulocytosis.
PTU: An antithyroid medication that blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and reduces peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
Monitor for severe liver injury and agranulocytosis.
levothyroxine: A synthetic form of thyroid hormone (T4) used to treat hypothyroidism.
Take consistently on an empty stomach, usually 30–60 minutes before breakfast, and separate from calcium or iron by about 4 hours. Monitor TSH.
hyperparathyroidism: Excess parathyroid hormone activity, usually causing elevated blood calcium.
Possible findings include kidney stones, bone pain, constipation, weakness, and confusion. Monitor calcium and renal status.
hypoparathyroidism: Insufficient parathyroid hormone, causing low blood calcium and often high phosphate.
Watch for perioral tingling, muscle cramps, tetany, positive Chvostek or Trousseau signs, seizures, and laryngospasm.
hypocalcemia: A lower-than-normal calcium level in the blood.
Can cause numbness, tingling, muscle cramps, tetany, seizures, and laryngospasm. IV calcium gluconate may be required for severe symptomatic cases.
cinacalcet: A calcimimetic medication that lowers parathyroid hormone secretion and serum calcium.
Monitor calcium because hypocalcemia can occur. Teach the client to report tingling, cramps, or muscle spasms.
diabetes insipidus: A disorder of water balance in which the kidneys cannot conserve water because of inadequate ADH action, causing large amounts of dilute urine.
Expect polyuria, intense thirst, low urine specific gravity, and possible dehydration/hypernatremia. Monitor intake/output, sodium, weight, and urine concentration.
central DI: Diabetes insipidus caused by inadequate production or release of antidiuretic hormone from the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary.
Desmopressin replaces ADH activity. Monitor urine output, urine concentration, sodium, and for water retention/hyponatremia.
nephrogenic DI: Diabetes insipidus in which the kidneys do not respond appropriately to ADH.
Desmopressin is usually ineffective. Review causes such as lithium or kidney disease; treatment may include adequate water and selected medications.
SIADH: Excess ADH activity causes the body to retain water, diluting serum sodium and producing concentrated urine.

Expect low serum sodium and osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine and often low urine output. Monitor neurologic status; fluid restriction is common, and severe symptoms may require carefully controlled hypertonic saline.
diabetic ketoacidosis: An acute complication of diabetes caused by severe insulin deficiency, leading to hyperglycemia, ketone production, and metabolic acidosis.
Assess glucose, ketones, anion gap, pH/bicarbonate, hydration, and potassium. Give IV fluids and insulin as prescribed; potassium must be monitored closely.
DKA: An acute diabetic emergency involving hyperglycemia, ketone production, dehydration, and metabolic acidosis.
Monitor glucose, potassium, ketones, anion gap, and acid-base status. Insulin shifts potassium into cells, so potassium must be assessed and corrected as ordered.
hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: A severe diabetic emergency characterized by profound hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration, usually with little or no significant ketoacidosis.
Priorities include fluid replacement, electrolyte monitoring, and insulin as prescribed. Assess mental status and circulation.
hypoglycemia: A blood glucose level that is lower than the safe target; in many adults, below 70 mg/dL is the alert threshold.
Symptoms can include sweating, tremor, hunger, palpitations, confusion, or seizures. Treat promptly using the client's ability to swallow and the prescribed protocol.
diabetic neuropathy: Nerve damage caused by prolonged diabetes, often affecting sensation in the feet and legs.
Loss of protective sensation increases risk of unnoticed injury and ulceration. Teach daily foot inspection and protective footwear.
desmopressin: A synthetic medication that acts like antidiuretic hormone, reducing urine production.
Used for central DI. Monitor urine output, weight, sodium, and signs of water retention or hyponatremia.
vasopressin antagonists: Medications that block ADH receptors, allowing the kidneys to excrete free water and raise serum sodium in selected cases of hyponatremia.
Monitor sodium correction closely because overly rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination. Tolvaptan has important liver and monitoring restrictions.
urine specific gravity: A measure of how concentrated or dilute urine is compared with water.
Very low values can occur with DI; concentrated urine is expected with SIADH. Interpret with fluid status and serum sodium/osmolality.
water-deprivation test: A supervised test that withholds fluids for a controlled period to evaluate the body's ability to concentrate urine.
It helps distinguish causes of polyuria such as DI and primary polydipsia. It requires close monitoring and must not be attempted at home.
hyponatremia: A lower-than-normal serum sodium concentration, often below 135 mEq/L.
Severe or rapidly developing hyponatremia can cause headache, confusion, seizures, and coma. Correct sodium carefully to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Guillain-Barré syndrome: An acute immune-mediated disorder in which the immune system attacks peripheral nerves, often causing ascending weakness and reduced reflexes.
The major danger is respiratory muscle weakness and autonomic instability. Monitor respiratory function, swallowing, heart rate, and blood pressure; IVIG or plasma exchange may be prescribed.
myasthenia gravis: An autoimmune disorder affecting communication between nerves and skeletal muscles, causing fluctuating weakness that worsens with activity.
Monitor swallowing, speech, respiratory effort, and fatigue. Time pyridostigmine so medication effect supports meals and activity as prescribed.
myasthenic crisis: Severe worsening of myasthenia gravis that causes respiratory muscle weakness and may lead to respiratory failure.
Prioritize airway and ventilation, monitor respiratory function and swallowing, and prepare for urgent escalation.
cholinergic crisis: Excess acetylcholine activity, often from too much acetylcholinesterase inhibitor medication, causing weakness and muscarinic symptoms.
Look for increased secretions, salivation, tearing, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, vomiting, bradycardia, and weakness. It requires urgent evaluation.
pyridostigmine: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction to improve muscle strength in myasthenia gravis.
Give on schedule and coordinate doses with meals when swallowing is difficult. Watch for excessive secretions, diarrhea, bradycardia, or worsening weakness.
rheumatoid arthritis: A chronic systemic autoimmune disease that causes inflammatory joint swelling, pain, stiffness, and progressive joint damage.
Morning stiffness and symmetric small-joint involvement are common. DMARDs reduce disease progression; fever or sore throat while immunosuppressed needs prompt follow-up.
rheumatoid factor: An autoantibody that may be present in rheumatoid arthritis and some other diseases.
A positive RF supports but does not prove RA; some people with RA are RF-negative, and RF can be positive in other conditions.
DMARDs: Medications that reduce inflammation and slow the progression of rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory rheumatic diseases.
They are not simply pain relievers. Monitor for infection, blood-count or liver abnormalities as appropriate to the specific drug.
methotrexate: An antimetabolite immunosuppressant commonly used weekly at low doses as a disease-modifying drug for rheumatoid arthritis.
For RA it is generally taken once weekly, not daily. Monitor CBC and liver function; report fever, sore throat, mouth sores, unusual bruising, or shortness of breath.
hydroxychloroquine: An antimalarial medication with immunomodulatory effects used for conditions such as SLE and rheumatoid arthritis.
It can reduce lupus flares and joint/skin symptoms. Baseline and regular retinal examinations are important because retinal toxicity can cause vision loss.
Sjögren syndrome: An autoimmune disease that commonly damages moisture-producing glands, causing dry eyes and dry mouth.
Assess for dental problems, difficulty swallowing dry foods, eye irritation, and systemic manifestations.
angioedema: Rapid swelling of deeper skin or mucosal tissues, often involving the lips, tongue, face, or throat.
Tongue or throat swelling, voice change, stridor, or difficulty breathing is an airway emergency. ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema even without hives.
anaphylaxis: A rapid, severe, potentially life-threatening systemic allergic reaction that can impair breathing and circulation.

Give IM epinephrine promptly in the mid-outer thigh, activate emergency response, support airway/breathing/circulation, and repeat epinephrine as directed. Antihistamines are not a substitute for epinephrine.
epinephrine: A catecholamine medication that stimulates alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors, increasing vascular tone, supporting cardiac output, and opening the airways.
IM epinephrine is first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer promptly in the mid-outer thigh; monitor airway, breathing, circulation, blood pressure, and response.
antihistamines: Medications that block histamine receptors and reduce symptoms such as itching, sneezing, hives, and runny nose.
They may help skin/nasal symptoms in allergic reactions but do not treat airway obstruction or shock in anaphylaxis; epinephrine is first-line.
immunosuppressants: Medications that reduce immune-system activity to treat autoimmune disease or prevent transplant rejection.
They increase infection risk and may affect blood counts, liver, or kidneys depending on the drug. Teach infection precautions and prompt reporting of fever.
calcineurin inhibitors: Immunosuppressant medications such as tacrolimus and cyclosporine that reduce T-cell activation by blocking calcineurin signaling.
Monitor drug levels when ordered, kidney function, blood pressure, electrolytes, and infection risk. These drugs can be nephrotoxic.
monoclonal antibodies: Laboratory-produced antibodies designed to bind a specific target, such as an immune-cell receptor or inflammatory protein.
They are used in autoimmune disease, cancer, and other conditions. Risks vary by drug but can include infusion reactions and serious infection.
CD4 count: The number of CD4 T-helper lymphocytes in a volume of blood, used to assess immune function in a person with HIV.
A declining count indicates immune damage. A count below 200 cells/mm³ is one criterion for AIDS and signals high risk for opportunistic infections.
viral load: The amount of HIV RNA measured in the blood.
It is used to monitor response to antiretroviral therapy. Effective treatment aims to suppress the viral load to an undetectable level.
antiretroviral therapy: Combination medication treatment that suppresses HIV replication and protects immune function.
Adherence is essential even when the person feels well. ART reduces viral load, improves CD4 status, and lowers transmission risk when viral suppression is maintained.
opportunistic infection: An infection that occurs more easily or severely when the immune system is weakened.
People with advanced HIV or medication-related immunosuppression are at increased risk. Prevention and early recognition are important.
meningitis: Inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord, often caused by infection.
Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status are concerning. Suspected bacterial meningitis requires urgent treatment and appropriate precautions.
sinusitis: Inflammation of the lining of the paranasal sinuses, often following a viral upper-respiratory infection.
Symptoms can include nasal congestion, facial pressure/pain, thick nasal drainage, and reduced smell.
antimicrobial stewardship: Using antibiotics and other antimicrobials only when appropriate, with the right drug, dose, route, and duration.
It reduces adverse effects, resistance, and unnecessary treatment. Obtain ordered cultures before antibiotics when this does not delay urgent care.
steroid taper: A gradual reduction in corticosteroid dose rather than stopping suddenly.
Long-term steroids suppress the body's own cortisol production. Abrupt discontinuation can trigger adrenal insufficiency or crisis.
somatropin: A recombinant form of human growth hormone used for selected growth hormone deficiencies and other approved indications.
Administer as prescribed and monitor growth, glucose, edema, joint pain, and signs of intracranial hypertension.
gabapentin: A medication used for neuropathic pain and certain seizure disorders.
It may cause dizziness, sleepiness, and impaired coordination. Use caution with other sedatives and assess fall risk.
pregabalin: A medication used for neuropathic pain and certain seizure disorders.
It may cause dizziness, drowsiness, edema, and weight gain. Use caution with sedatives and assess fall risk.
calcium gluconate: An IV calcium salt used to treat severe symptomatic hypocalcemia and to stabilize the cardiac membrane in severe hyperkalemia.
Administer at the prescribed rate with cardiac monitoring when indicated; assess IV site because extravasation can injure tissue.
Chvostek sign: Facial muscle twitching after tapping the facial nerve, which can occur with hypocalcemia.
It may support concern for neuromuscular irritability but is not diagnostic by itself.
Trousseau sign: Carpal spasm triggered by inflating a blood-pressure cuff, associated with neuromuscular irritability from hypocalcemia.
A positive sign can occur with low calcium and should prompt assessment of calcium and symptoms.
tetany: Involuntary muscle contractions or spasms caused by increased nerve and muscle excitability, often from low calcium.
Watch for cramps, tingling, carpopedal spasm, seizures, or laryngospasm in severe hypocalcemia.
paresthesia: An abnormal sensation such as tingling, prickling, or numbness.
Perioral or hand tingling can be an early sign of hypocalcemia.
agranulocytosis: A dangerously low number of neutrophils, greatly increasing the risk of severe infection.
Fever, sore throat, or mouth ulcers while taking methimazole or PTU require prompt evaluation and a CBC.
thionamide: A class of antithyroid medications, including methimazole and propylthiouracil, that inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis.
Teach clients to report fever or sore throat because agranulocytosis is a rare but serious adverse effect.
thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of all or part of the thyroid gland.
After surgery, monitor airway, bleeding, voice, and calcium. Keep emergency airway equipment and calcium treatment available as ordered.
parathyroidectomy: Surgical removal of one or more parathyroid glands, often to treat hyperparathyroidism.
Monitor calcium closely after surgery because hypocalcemia can cause tingling, tetany, seizures, or laryngospasm.
hypertonic saline: A concentrated sodium chloride IV solution, such as 3% saline, used for selected severe symptomatic hyponatremia cases.
Administer with close monitoring of sodium and neurologic status. Avoid correcting sodium too rapidly because osmotic demyelination can occur.
osmotic demyelination: A serious neurologic injury that can occur when chronic hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly, damaging myelin in the brain.
Prevent it by following controlled sodium-correction limits and frequent laboratory monitoring.
exophthalmos: Forward protrusion of one or both eyeballs, commonly associated with Graves disease.
Protect the eyes from dryness and injury; assess vision changes and ability to close the eyelids.
thyrotoxicosis: A clinical state caused by excessive thyroid hormone action in the body, regardless of the source.
Severe thyrotoxicosis can progress to thyroid storm, with fever, marked tachycardia, and altered mental status.
hypokalemia: A lower-than-normal potassium level in the blood.
Can cause muscle weakness, cramps, constipation, and dangerous dysrhythmias. Monitor ECG and replace potassium as prescribed.
hyperkalemia: A higher-than-normal potassium level in the blood.
Can cause life-threatening cardiac conduction changes and dysrhythmias. Assess ECG and treat urgently when severe.
polyuria: Production of an abnormally large volume of urine.
It is common in diabetes mellitus with hyperglycemia and in diabetes insipidus due to impaired water conservation.
polydipsia: Excessive thirst or increased fluid intake.
It often accompanies polyuria in diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus.
osmolality: The concentration of dissolved particles per kilogram of water, commonly measured in serum or urine.
Serum osmolality is often high in DI and low in SIADH. Interpret alongside sodium, urine osmolality, and volume status.
